scenario.name: SolarWinds SUNSPOT Build Hijack & SUNBURST Backdoor (APT29)
scenario.overview: Picture an active industrial factory floor with a moving assembly conveyor belt, an articulated yellow robotic arm, steel parts bins, and a final quality-seal stamping desk. During the quiet night shift on the factory floor, a saboteur steps beside the moving assembly conveyor right before the automated quality stamp. In this real-world scenario, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the factory quality stamp station in tiny disguised batches, then approaches the factory quality stamp station disguised as a regular visitor. Only when a quality engineer checks the finished product’s weight and internal wiring against the locked master blueprint cabinet does the factory-line swap appear. In this scenario (T1195.002, SolarWinds SUNSPOT Build Hijack & SUNBURST Backdoor (APT29)), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: sUNSPOT Build-Time Source Injection, then sUNBURST Dormancy, FNV-1a Blocklist Check, then tEARDROP Memory-Only Dropper. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering SUNSPOT Build-Time Source Injection, then SUNBURST Dormancy, FNV-1a Blocklist Check, then TEARDROP Memory-Only Dropper, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 11 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: Stage 1: SUNSPOT Build-Time Source Injection into MSBuild
stages.subtitle: Initial Access (T1195.002 - Compromise Software Supply Chain)
stages.description: During the quiet night shift on the factory floor, a saboteur steps beside the moving assembly conveyor right before the automated quality stamp. Specifically in Step 1, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the factory quality stamp station in tiny disguised batches while everyday visitors and the factory quality inspector go about their routine. APT29 deployed SUNSPOT (taskhostsvc.exe, a custom build-hijacking service that polls running processes every second for MsBuild.exe) onto the SolarWinds Orion build server. When a build of SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.csproj began, SUNSPOT temporarily replaced InventoryManager.cs on disk (injecting the OrionImprovementBusinessLayer backdoor class right before the C# compiler read the file and restoring the original file immediately after compilation) so zero malicious commits ever appeared in the source control repository. SUNSPOT checks the command-line arguments of MsBuild.exe, verifies target file hashes with MD5, acquires a mutex, replaces InventoryManager.cs, logs any compilation errors to an AES-encrypted log at C:\Windows\Temp\vmware-vmdmp.log, and restores the original .cs file before the build finishes and enters the code-signing step. In the documented EventID 11 exchange from APT29 C2 (*.avsvmcloud.com) to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK 11 (confirming that the C:\Windows\System32\taskhostsvc.exe (SUNSPOT build monitor) request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: SUNBURST Dormancy, FNV-1a Blocklist Check & DGA C2 Beacon). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ C:\Windows\System32\taskhostsvc.exe (SUNSPOT build monitor) / ⇠#1 ACK 11) from Node ① (#1 APT29 C2 (*.avsvmcloud.com)) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 AD Federation Services (SAML)).

stages.title: Stage 2: SUNBURST Dormancy, FNV-1a Blocklist Check & DGA C2 Beacon
stages.subtitle: Command and Control (T1568.002 - Domain Generation Algorithms)
stages.description: The robotic arm pauses for a heartbeat as the saboteur swaps one genuine component on the belt for an identical-looking counterfeit part carrying a hidden wire. Here in Step 2 inside the factory floor, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the factory quality stamp station in tiny disguised batches without disturbing the original master blueprint cabinet. When customers installed the signed Orion update, SolarWinds.BusinessLayerHost.exe loaded the trojanized DLL. SUNBURST enforced a 12-to-14-day dormancy period, hashed running processes, services, and drivers using 64-bit FNV-1a + XOR (comparing them against hardcoded hashes of EDR and analysis tools without storing plaintext process names in the binary), and then issued a DNS query to *.avsvmcloud.com (encoding the victim’s Active Directory domain name and MAC address into the subdomain label). By encoding the victim’s internal domain name into the DNS DGA query, APT29 could passively inspect DNS lookups at their authoritative nameserver and selectively reply with a CNAME record pointing to a Stage-2 server only for high-value government and technology targets. In the documented EventID 22 exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to TeamCity / MSBuild Server, TeamCity / MSBuild Server responds with ACK 22 (confirming that the SolarWinds.BusinessLayerHost.exe request succeeded on TeamCity / MSBuild Server and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: TEARDROP Memory-Only Dropper & ADFS Golden SAML Theft). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ SolarWinds.BusinessLayerHost.exe / ⇠#2 ACK 22) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 TeamCity / MSBuild Server), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 AD Federation Services (SAML)).

stages.title: Stage 3: TEARDROP Memory-Only Dropper & ADFS Golden SAML Theft
stages.subtitle: Credential Access (T1552.004 - Private Keys / Golden SAML)
stages.description: The assembly line rolls forward, the factory press stamps the official warranty seal right onto the tampered unit, and trucks ship it to every trusting customer. In this final step inside the factory floor, the intruder approaches the factory quality stamp station disguised as a regular visitor until the assembly line inspection camera catches the mismatch. For selected victims, SUNBURST communicated over HTTPS disguised as SolarWinds Orion Improvement Program (OIP) JSON telemetry, deployed the memory-only TEARDROP dropper via Image File Execution Options (IFEO) (registering a debugger hijack that loaded a custom Cobalt Strike Beacon from a fake JPEG file in RAM), and laterally moved to the ADFS server to extract the token-signing private key (Golden SAML, enabling the attacker to forge cryptographically valid SAML assertions for any cloud user without touching Active Directory passwords). Using the stolen ADFS EncryptedPFX blob and Distributed Key Manager (DKM) decryption key from Active Directory, the attacker mints arbitrary SAML 2.0 tokens offline to access Microsoft 365 and Azure resources. In the documented EventID 13 exchange from TeamCity / MSBuild Server to Orion Server (BusinessLayerHost), Orion Server (BusinessLayerHost) responds with ALERT 13 (confirming that the SolarWinds.BusinessLayerHost.exe request succeeded on Orion Server (BusinessLayerHost) and completing the final execution objective of SolarWinds SUNSPOT Build Hijack & SUNBURST Backdoor (APT29)). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ SolarWinds.BusinessLayerHost.exe / ⇠#3 ALERT 13) from Node ③ (#3 TeamCity / MSBuild Server) to Node ④ (#4 Orion Server (BusinessLayerHost)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 AD Federation Services (SAML)).
